title: The Pursuit & the Ending
content_html:
The Murder of Elizabeth

On his wedding night, Victor arms himself and patrols the house, convinced the Creature’s threat was directed at him. He leaves Elizabeth alone in their room. When he hears her scream, he rushes in to find her dead: “She was there, lifeless and inanimate, thrown across the bed, her head hanging down and her pale and distorted features half covered by her hair.” The Gothic imagery — the lifeless body, distorted features, hair covering the face — mirrors the creation scene in reverse: where Victor once brought dead matter to life, the Creature now brings death to the living.

Victor’s failure to protect Elizabeth is a structural echo of his failure to nurture the Creature. In both cases, he is absorbed in his own concerns and fails to see the obvious threat. The Creature watches through the window, “a grin on its face,” paralleling the “grin” it wore at its creation. Shelley closes the circle: the smile the creator rejected has become the smile of the destroyer. Everything the Creature was denied — love, a partner, a wedding night — it now takes from Victor.

Key Fact

Elizabeth’s murder is the creation scene in reverse: Victor once brought dead matter to life; now the Creature brings death to life. The Creature’s grin through the window echoes its newborn smile, turning innocence into menace. Victor’s failure to protect Elizabeth mirrors his failure to nurture the Creature — in both cases, his self-absorption leads to destruction.

The Arctic Pursuit

After Elizabeth’s death and his father’s death from grief, Victor pursues the Creature across Europe and into the Arctic. The pursuit reverses their original roles: Victor, the creator, is now the one chasing; the Creature, once the pursuer of human connection, now flees. The Arctic setting is sublime — vast, desolate, and utterly indifferent to human suffering. Shelley places the final confrontation in the most inhospitable landscape on Earth, symbolising the emotional wasteland both characters now inhabit.

The Creature leaves food for Victor along the trail, keeping him alive so the pursuit can continue. This detail is deeply disturbing: the Creature wants Victor to suffer as long as possible. But it can also be read as the Creature’s last perverse act of connection — Victor is the only being who acknowledges the Creature’s existence. Their relationship, however destructive, is the only relationship either of them has left.

Victor dies aboard Walton’s ship, exhausted by the pursuit. His final words to Walton are telling: even on his deathbed, he cannot decide whether his creation was right or wrong. He warns Walton against ambition but also says: “Another may succeed where I have failed.” This ambiguity is deliberate — Shelley refuses to give Victor a neat moral resolution. He dies as he lived: brilliant, tormented, and unable to take full responsibility for what he has done.

The Creature’s Final Speech

The Creature appears over Victor’s dead body and delivers its final speech to Walton. This is one of the most powerful passages in the novel. The Creature mourns Victor: “That is also my victim! In his murder my crimes are consummated.” The word “consummated” (meaning completed or fulfilled) links death to marriage, echoing the wedding-night murder. The Creature is not triumphant — it is devastated. Revenge brought no satisfaction, only emptier isolation.

The Creature declares it will travel to the “most northern extremity of the globe” and build its own funeral pyre: “I shall die. I shall no longer feel the agonies which now consume me.” It leaps from the ship window and is “borne away by the waves and lost in darkness and distance.” Shelley ends the novel with ambiguity: we do not see the Creature die. It vanishes into the sublime Arctic, leaving the reader to wonder whether it truly ends or continues to haunt the edges of the world.

Key Fact

The Creature’s final speech reveals that revenge brought no peace: “In his murder my crimes are consummated” shows recognition that destroying Victor destroyed the Creature’s last connection to another being. The planned funeral pyre represents the Creature’s only remaining choice: self-destruction. Shelley’s message is that the cycle of revenge ultimately annihilates both creator and creation.

The novel ends where it began: with Walton in the Arctic. His crew demand they turn back south. Walton must decide whether to continue his dangerous quest or heed Victor’s warning. Shelley leaves this choice ambiguous, returning the moral question to the reader. Will humanity learn from Victor’s mistake? Will ambition be tempered by responsibility? The open ending suggests Shelley was not optimistic — the desire to push beyond limits is part of human nature. The novel is a warning, but it is uncertain whether the warning will be heard.

title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
content_html:
The Five Major Themes

Every essay on Frankenstein connects to one or more key themes. The five most commonly tested are: dangerous knowledge and ambition, creation and responsibility, monstrosity and prejudice, isolation and companionship, and nature versus nurture.

Key Fact

Dangerous Knowledge: "So much has been done — far more will I achieve" (Victor's Promethean ambition). Creation & Responsibility: "A new species would bless me as its creator" (Victor wants worship, not responsibility). Monstrosity: "I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open" (the pronoun 'it' dehumanises from birth). Isolation: "I am alone and miserable" (the Creature's plea for a companion). Nature vs Nurture: "From that moment I declared everlasting war against the species" (society creates the monster).

Key Quotations Bank

"A new species would bless me as its creator and source." — Victor's hubris: he wants godlike worship.

"Workshop of filthy creation" — "filthy" reveals Victor's subconscious disgust at his own work.

"Breathless horror and disgust filled my heart." — Victor's immediate rejection of his creation.

"Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay to mould me man?" — The Creature quotes Paradise Lost, challenging Victor's right to create and abandon.

"I am alone and miserable; man will not associate with me." — The Creature's most sympathetic plea.

"I shall be with you on your wedding-night." — The Creature's threat, creating dramatic irony.

"In his murder my crimes are consummated." — Revenge brings no peace; "consummated" links death and marriage.

"Everywhere I see bliss, from which I alone am irrevocably excluded." — The Creature's awareness of its permanent isolation.

What the 19th-Century Novel Question Tests

Your response is assessed on three strands: your critical response to the text with well-chosen references (AO1), your analysis of the writer's methods — language, structure and form (AO2), and your understanding of context (AO3). You will receive a printed extract (~400 words) and must write about the extract AND the novel as a whole. Check your exam board's specimen paper and mark scheme for the exact weightings and timings that apply to your exam.

Key Fact

AO1 — Critical response: Build a clear argument supported by well-chosen references from the extract AND the whole novel. AO2 — Writer's methods: Analyse Shelley's methods — language, structure, narrative voice, symbolism. AO3 — Context: Embed context (Enlightenment, Romanticism, Gothic, biography). Never bolt context on as a separate paragraph.

Essay Structure

Use PEALCE: Point → Evidence → Analyse Language → Link to Context → Evaluate. Balance extract analysis (2–3 paragraphs) with whole-novel references (2–3 paragraphs). The biggest mark differentiator is close analysis of methods — analyse what they do, don't just identify them.

Point: Shelley presents Victor's rejection of the Creature as an act of parental failure. Evidence: "I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open; it breathed hard." Analysis: The pronoun "it" immediately dehumanises the Creature, denying it personhood. The focus on a single "dull yellow eye" reduces the being to one unsettling detail, reflecting Victor's inability to see beyond surface appearance. The passive phrasing — "it breathed" rather than "he breathed" — distances Victor from responsibility. Context: Shelley, whose own mother died in childbirth, was deeply aware that creation carries moral obligations. Victor's rejection of a conscious being echoes the Enlightenment's blind faith in progress without consideration of consequences. Evaluate: This moment establishes Shelley's central argument: the true horror is not the Creature's appearance but the creator's refusal to take responsibility.

title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
content_html:
Theme 1: Ambition

Ambition is the play’s driving force. Macbeth’s “vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself” (Act 1, Scene 7) is his sole acknowledged motive. The horse-leaping metaphor captures how overreaching ambition destroys itself. Lady Macbeth’s ambition is equally fierce: “Glamis thou art, and Cawdor; and shalt be / What thou art promised” (Act 1, Scene 5). She treats the prophecy as a certainty and the murder as a practical step, not a moral crime. Shakespeare shows that ambition without moral restraint leads to tyranny, isolation, and self-destruction.

Theme 2: Guilt

Guilt manifests differently in the two protagonists. Macbeth’s guilt is immediate and overwhelming: the dagger hallucination (Act 2, Scene 1), “Sleep no more” (Act 2, Scene 2), “Neptune’s ocean” (Act 2, Scene 2), Banquo’s ghost (Act 3, Scene 4). Lady Macbeth’s guilt is suppressed then catastrophic: she dismisses it in Act 2 (“a little water”) but is destroyed by it in Act 5 (“Out, damned spot!”). Shakespeare presents guilt as inescapable — it cannot be washed, buried, or dismissed. For a Jacobean audience, this reflects the belief that sin inevitably brings divine punishment.

Key Fact

Guilt is inescapable in Macbeth. Macbeth’s guilt is immediate (dagger, “Neptune’s ocean”, Banquo’s ghost); Lady Macbeth’s is delayed but devastating (“a little water” → “Out, damned spot”). Their contrasting timelines create the play’s chiasmus structure. AO4: Jacobean belief that sin brings divine punishment.

Theme 3: Power and Kingship

Shakespeare contrasts legitimate and illegitimate power. Duncan rules with “faculties so meek” — gentle, God-ordained authority that makes Scotland flourish (“I have begun to plant thee”). Macbeth’s tyranny makes Scotland bleed (“bleed, bleed, poor country”, Act 4, Scene 3). Malcolm defines the “king-becoming graces” that Macbeth lacks. The play’s political message: power obtained through regicide is always illegitimate, and divine order will always be restored.

The supernatural raises the play’s central philosophical question: is Macbeth controlled by fate (the witches determine his future) or free will (he chooses to murder)? The witches never tell Macbeth to kill — they prophesy, and he acts. The “horrid image” of murder comes from within him (Act 1, Scene 3). The self-fulfilling prophecy interpretation suggests the witches merely activate an ambition already present. A Jacobean audience would likely have seen both: the witches as real supernatural agents AND Macbeth as a man who freely chose damnation.

Theme 5: Masculinity

Masculinity is weaponised throughout the play. Lady Macbeth attacks Macbeth’s manhood (“When you durst do it, then you were a man”, Act 1, Scene 7). Macbeth uses the same tactic on the murderers (“Are you so gospelled?”, Act 3, Scene 1). Violence becomes the measure of manhood. Shakespeare offers an alternative through Macduff: “I must also feel it as a man” (Act 4, Scene 3) insists that genuine masculinity includes emotional depth, not just aggression.

Key Fact

The six key themes: ambition (“vaulting ambition”), guilt (“Neptune’s ocean” / “damned spot”), power and kingship (Duncan vs Macbeth’s rule), the supernatural and fate vs free will (prophecies vs choice), masculinity (“when you durst do it” / “feel it as a man”), and appearance vs reality (“fair is foul”). For the exam, you need quotations and context for each.

Shakespeare Exam Technique

Your Shakespeare paper will typically give you a printed extract and ask you to respond in two connected tasks: (i) close analysis of the extract — focus on language and structure, name techniques, quote evidence and explain effects; and (ii) theme or character elsewhere in the play — range across the whole play and embed context. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact wording, timings and mark weightings.

Many Shakespeare papers are closed book, so you must memorise quotations. Aim for 5-8 short, versatile quotations per character/theme that you can deploy in different questions. Split your time evenly between the two tasks. Write 3-4 paragraphs per part, each with a clear point, evidence, and analysis.

Point: Shakespeare presents Macbeth as consumed by guilt through the dagger hallucination. Evidence: “Is this a dagger which I see before me, / The handle toward my hand?” Analysis (AO2): The dagger’s handle pointing toward Macbeth suggests the murder is being offered to him. The question form shows uncertainty and loss of control. As the vision develops “gouts of blood,” Shakespeare shows that guilt is already overwhelming Macbeth before the act itself. Development: The hallucination’s ambiguity (supernatural or psychological) reflects the play’s central question about whether Macbeth is controlled by external forces or his own desires.

Point: Shakespeare presents guilt as inescapable through the blood motif. Evidence: “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood clean from my hand?” (Act 2, Scene 2). Analysis (AO2): The hyperbole suggests guilt exceeds all nature. “Incardnadine” (Latinate) contrasts with “making the green one red” (Anglo-Saxon), showing horror stripping away eloquence. Context (AO4): Macbeth appeals to Neptune, a pagan god, rather than the Christian God — a Jacobean audience would recognise this as spiritual damnation. Regicide cuts Macbeth off from divine grace. Link: This is reversed in Lady Macbeth’s sleepwalking (“All the perfumes of Arabia”, Act 5, Scene 1), creating the play’s chiasmus of guilt.

title: Acts 1-2: The Decision for War
content_html:
The Salic Law Speech: Justifying War

Act 1 opens with the Archbishop of Canterbury delivering a famously tedious speech about the Salic Law to justify Henry’s claim to the French throne. The speech is so convoluted that audiences often cannot follow it — and Shakespeare may have intended this. Canterbury and the Bishop of Ely have a private conversation beforehand (Act 1, Scene 1) revealing that they support the war partly to protect Church lands from a parliamentary bill. The legal justification for war is tangled with self-interest. Shakespeare invites the audience to question whether the cause is just from the very beginning.

Henry appears to demand certainty: “May I with right and conscience make this claim?” He insists Canterbury take “heed how you awake our sleeping sword of war” and warns him that the deaths of soldiers will be on Canterbury’s conscience. Shakespeare presents Henry as a king who wants moral clarity — but he asks the question of a man who has a financial incentive to give the answer he wants. The structural irony is sharp: the audience can see what Henry apparently cannot (or will not).

Key Fact

Canterbury supports the war partly to protect Church lands from a parliamentary bill. His Salic Law speech is deliberately convoluted. Shakespeare creates structural irony: Henry asks for moral guidance from men with political motives to encourage war. The justice of Henry’s cause is questionable from Act 1.

The Tennis Balls: Insult & Transformation

The French Dauphin sends Henry a gift of tennis balls, mocking him as a frivolous young man better suited to games than politics. Henry’s response is one of the play’s most powerful speeches: “tell the pleasant Prince this mock of his / Hath turned his balls to gun-stones.” The pun on “balls” is deliberate: the Dauphin’s joke becomes a threat of artillery. Henry transforms a personal insult into a justification for war, promising that “many a thousand widows / Shall this his mock mock out of their dear husbands.”

The speech reveals Henry’s rhetorical brilliance. He shifts the moral responsibility for the war onto the Dauphin: it is the insult, not Henry’s ambition, that causes the invasion. This is a political performance — Henry frames his decision to invade France as a response to provocation rather than an act of aggression. Shakespeare allows the audience to admire the rhetoric while questioning whether it is genuine or calculated.

In Act 2, Scene 2, Henry exposes three traitors — Cambridge, Scroop and Grey — who have been bribed by the French to assassinate him. Henry traps them brilliantly: he asks their advice about pardoning a man who insulted him, and when they argue for severity, he turns their own argument against them. “The mercy that was quick in us but late, / By your own counsel is suppressed and killed.” The scene reveals Henry as a cold, calculating strategist who uses performance to control others. His betrayal by Scroop — a close personal friend — is the one moment where genuine emotion breaks through: “I will weep for thee; / For this revolt of thine, methinks, is like / Another fall of man.” The religious language (“fall of man”) elevates personal betrayal to cosmic significance.

The Death of Falstaff (Act 2, Scene 3)

Falstaff never appears in Henry V, but his death is reported by Mistress Quickly in one of Shakespeare’s most moving passages: “his nose was as sharp as a pen, and ’a babbled of green fields.” The audience knows from Henry IV Part 2 that Henry rejected Falstaff publicly (“I know thee not, old man”), and Quickly says Falstaff’s heart was “fracted and corroborate” (broken). Falstaff’s death is the cost of Henry’s transformation from wild prince to disciplined king. Shakespeare does not let the audience forget that Henry’s kingship was purchased at the expense of human warmth.

Key Fact

Falstaff dies off-stage, broken by Henry’s rejection. His death symbolises the sacrifice of personal warmth and private humanity that Henry’s kingship demands. Shakespeare shows that to become the ideal public king, Henry must kill the private man he once was.

Falstaff’s former companions — Bardolph, Pistol and Nym — go to war in France, but they are cowards and thieves, not heroes. They provide a comic counterpoint to Henry’s noble speeches: while Henry talks of honour, Pistol talks of profit. Bardolph is later hanged for stealing from a church — and Henry, who once drank with him, allows the execution without mercy: “We would have all such offenders so cut off.” Shakespeare uses the underworld characters to show that war is not all heroism — for ordinary soldiers, it is brutality, opportunism and death.

title: Part 2: Foster Care & Maureen
content_html:
Separation: The System Divides

Part 2 opens with the event that defines the rest of the novel: Leon and Jake are separated. Jake — white, a baby, and therefore ‘more adoptable’ in the language of the system — is placed with a middle-class adoptive family. Leon is placed with foster carer Maureen. The separation is presented as a bureaucratic decision, made in an office, without Leon’s consent or understanding.

Key Fact

Jake is adopted quickly because he is white and a baby — the two characteristics that made children most ‘placeable’ in the 1980s care system. Leon is older, mixed-race, and emotionally damaged. The system sees Jake as an easy success and Leon as a difficult case.

De Waal presents the separation without melodrama. Leon is simply told, in careful language, that Jake is going to live with another family. He doesn’t fully understand that this is permanent. The restraint of the prose makes the scene more devastating — Leon’s silence and confusion speak louder than tears would.

Maureen: Warmth and Stability

Maureen is a Jamaican-British woman who has fostered many children. She is warm, practical, and loving — the opposite of the cold institutional world Leon has just experienced. Her home smells of cooking. She feeds Leon properly. She calls him “sweetheart.” She represents the diaspora community — people who understand racial identity and cultural belonging in ways the white care system does not.

Sensory language: Maureen’s home is presented through warmth, food, and colour. De Waal uses the semantic field of nourishment — both physical and emotional — to contrast with the deprivation of Leon’s previous life.

Cultural identity: Maureen gives Leon something the system cannot — a connection to his Black heritage. She cooks Caribbean food, uses Jamaican dialect, and normalises his mixed-race identity in ways that no social worker has done.

Patience: Maureen doesn’t push Leon to talk or perform gratitude. She allows him space to grieve. Her parenting style is instinctive and community-based, contrasting with the social workers’ procedural approach.

Limitations: Despite her warmth, Maureen cannot fix the fundamental problem — Leon wants Jake, and she cannot give him that. This creates an ongoing tension: Leon loves Maureen but cannot let go of his brother.

Leon’s Internal Conflict

Part 2 is dominated by Leon’s struggle between two impulses: settling into Maureen’s home and refusing to accept the loss of Jake. He begins to form attachments — to Maureen, to the garden, to routines — but guilt pulls him back. Accepting Maureen feels like betraying Jake and Carol.

Key Fact

De Waal presents Leon’s internal conflict through behaviour rather than explicit thought. He acts out, tests boundaries, and oscillates between warmth and withdrawal. His anger is never fully explained to other characters because he lacks the vocabulary to articulate his grief.

Leon’s behaviour in Part 2 includes stealing, lying, and occasional violence. De Waal never presents these as moral failings. Instead, they are shown as the logical responses of a traumatised child trying to regain control over a world that has taken everything from him. The reader is positioned to understand what the system might label as ‘difficult behaviour’ is actually trauma response.

Maureen’s garden becomes a central symbol in Part 2. Leon works in the garden, planting seeds and watching things grow. The garden represents nurture, patience, and the possibility of putting down roots. It offers Leon a form of agency — he can care for something and see results.

However, the garden is also temporary. Leon knows he is in foster care, not adopted. Everything he plants could be taken away, just as Jake was taken. De Waal uses the garden to explore the tension between hope and impermanence that defines the foster care experience.

Contact Visits and Diminishing Hope

Leon is allowed contact visits with Jake, but these become less frequent over time. Each visit is both joyful and agonising — Leon sees Jake changing, growing, becoming part of another family. The visits are supervised, timed, and controlled by adults. Leon has no power over when he sees his brother or for how long.

De Waal uses the diminishing visits structurally: as the gaps between contact grow longer, the reader feels Leon’s grip on his brother loosening. The system is slowly, bureaucratically erasing the sibling bond — not through cruelty, but through process.

title: Character Analysis
content_html:
Characters in Journey’s End

Sherriff populates his dugout with a carefully chosen group of characters who represent different responses to war. For the Edexcel exam, you need to be able to write about how each character is presented, what they reveal about the play’s themes, and how Sherriff uses them to explore the effects of conflict on individuals. Remember that Section B tests AO1 (your response and use of quotations) and AO3 (context), so always link character analysis to the historical period.

Captain Stanhope

Stanhope is the protagonist and the most complex character in the play. He is twenty-one years old, has been at the front for three years without leave, and is the longest-serving officer in the battalion. He is a brilliant and dedicated commander — the Colonel calls him “the best company commander in the battalion” — but he is also an alcoholic who drinks to suppress the psychological damage of prolonged combat.

Stanhope’s central conflict is between the person he was (a popular, heroic schoolboy) and the person the war has made him (a traumatised, dependent wreck). His fear about Raleigh’s letter reveals this split: he is terrified that his fiancée Madge will learn the truth. His line “You think there’s no limit to what a man can bear?” is the play’s most direct expression of psychological breaking point.

Key Fact

Stanhope’s alcoholism is not weakness but survival. He says: “It’s the only way to forget.” Sherriff presents a young man who has been pushed beyond his limits by a war that offers no support for mental health. His fierce loyalty, his tenderness with the dying Raleigh, and his refusal to leave the front all show that duty and damage can coexist.

Osborne is the oldest officer in the company, a former schoolmaster and rugby player, and the emotional heart of the group. He is nicknamed “uncle” because of his paternal, caring nature. He defends Stanhope to Hardy, reassures Raleigh, reads Alice in Wonderland, and organises earwig races — small acts of kindness that hold the group together.

Osborne represents the gentlemanly ideal: calm, decent, selfless. His death during the raid is the play’s emotional turning point. Sherriff kills the most universally loved character to show that war does not spare the good. Osborne’s reading of Alice in Wonderland before the raid connects his innocence to the absurdity of the world he is about to enter — a world where decency offers no protection.

Second Lieutenant Raleigh

Raleigh is the youngest and most inexperienced officer, fresh from England and eager to serve. He hero-worships Stanhope from their school days and pulled strings to be posted to his company. Raleigh functions as the audience’s entry point into the world of the trenches: his naïveté mirrors our own unfamiliarity, and his gradual loss of innocence mirrors the broader disillusionment caused by the war.

Raleigh’s description of Stanhope as “the one man I could talk to as a friend” establishes the schoolboy bond that Stanhope fears the war has destroyed. His refusal to eat at the dinner after Osborne’s death shows genuine moral feeling, but also reveals his inability to understand the coping mechanisms that front-line soldiers need. His death on Osborne’s bed completes his journey from innocent to casualty, and Stanhope’s tenderness in that scene finally reconciles the two men.

Trotter is a cheerful, uncomplicated officer from a lower-middle-class background. He talks constantly about food, draws circles on a chart to count down the hours of each duty period, and provides comic relief through his blunt, good-natured personality. His coping mechanism is to focus on small, tangible pleasures — the next meal, the next rest period — rather than thinking about the bigger picture.

Trotter is often underestimated in exam answers, but he is important. He represents the ordinary soldier who survives by not thinking too deeply. His promotion to replace Osborne after the raid shows that the war values endurance over sensitivity. Sherriff uses Trotter to contrast with the more emotionally complex Stanhope and Osborne — his simplicity is both his strength and his limitation.

Second Lieutenant Hibbert

Hibbert is the most controversial character in the play. He claims to have neuralgia and asks to be sent to the rear, but Stanhope sees through his excuse and threatens to shoot him. Hibbert represents the fear that every soldier felt but most suppressed. His attempt to escape is not simply cowardice; it is a human response to intolerable conditions.

What makes Hibbert interesting is that Stanhope admits he has felt the same way. The difference between them is not that Stanhope is braver — it is that Stanhope’s sense of duty is stronger. Sherriff blurs the line between courage and cowardice, suggesting that both are responses to the same impossible situation. Hibbert challenges the audience to consider whether they would behave any differently.

Key Fact

Hibbert and Stanhope are two sides of the same coin. Both are terrified. Stanhope stays because of duty and alcohol; Hibbert tries to leave because he has no coping mechanism. Sherriff asks whether the line between courage and cowardice is really as clear as the military system demands.

Mason is the officers’ cook and batman. He provides gentle comic relief through his complaints about the quality of food (“a yellow sort of stuff, sir”) and his earnest attempts to make the best of terrible supplies. Mason humanises the dugout and reminds the audience that even in war, people cling to the routines of normal life.

The Colonel represents the military hierarchy. He orders the dangerous raid, dismisses Stanhope’s objections about sending Osborne, and sends champagne to celebrate the capture of a prisoner — apparently indifferent to Osborne’s death. The Colonel is not a villain, but his detachment from the human cost of his orders illustrates the gap between those who give commands and those who carry them out.

Together, these characters form a cross-section of the officer class: the heroic wreck (Stanhope), the steady mentor (Osborne), the innocent newcomer (Raleigh), the cheerful pragmatist (Trotter), the man at breaking point (Hibbert), and the detached authority (the Colonel). Each responds to the war differently, and Sherriff uses their contrasts to explore the full range of human responses to conflict.

title: Context: Republican Rome & Elizabethan England
content_html:
Why Shakespeare Wrote About Rome

Shakespeare wrote Julius Caesar around 1599, drawing heavily on Sir Thomas North’s English translation of Plutarch’s Lives of the Noble Greeks and Romans. Plutarch provided the historical detail — the assassination, the funeral speeches, the civil war — but Shakespeare transformed dry biography into a gripping political thriller. He compressed timelines, invented dialogue, and added dramatic devices like the soothsayer’s warning to heighten tension.

The play was first performed at the newly built Globe Theatre. It was one of Shakespeare’s most popular works in his lifetime, partly because Roman history was central to Elizabethan education. Grammar school students studied Plutarch, Cicero, and Seneca. An Elizabethan audience would have recognised the historical figures instantly and understood the political parallels Shakespeare was drawing.

Key Fact

Shakespeare’s primary source was Plutarch’s Lives, translated by Sir Thomas North in 1579. Some of Antony’s funeral speech is almost directly lifted from North’s translation, showing how closely Shakespeare worked from this source.

The Roman Republic

To understand the play, you need to understand what Rome was in 44 BC. Rome was a republic — a state governed not by a king but by elected senators and consuls. The Romans had overthrown their last king, Tarquin the Proud, in 509 BC and were fiercely proud of their republican system. The very idea of one man holding permanent, unchecked power was considered tyranny — the worst political crime imaginable.

Julius Caesar had been appointed ‘dictator perpetuo’ (dictator for life) by the Senate. To his supporters, he was a brilliant military leader who had expanded the empire and given land to soldiers and the poor. To his enemies, he was destroying the republic by concentrating power in himself. This is the central tension of the play: was Caesar a tyrant who deserved to die, or a great leader murdered by jealous men?

Senate: The governing body of Rome, made up of around 600 wealthy, aristocratic men (the patricians). Senators like Brutus and Cassius saw themselves as guardians of the republic.

Consul: The two annually elected leaders of Rome. Power was deliberately shared to prevent any one person becoming a king. Caesar’s appointment as permanent dictator violated this principle.

Plebeians: The common people of Rome. In the play, they are fickle and easily swayed — first cheering Brutus, then turning on the conspirators after Antony’s speech. Shakespeare uses them to explore how easily the public can be manipulated.

Elizabethan Parallels: Succession and Anxiety

Shakespeare was not writing about Rome for its own sake. In 1599, Queen Elizabeth I was sixty-six years old, unmarried, and had no heir. The question of who would succeed her dominated English politics. There was genuine fear that her death would trigger a power struggle, even civil war. A play about the assassination of a powerful leader and the chaos that followed would have felt dangerously relevant to an Elizabethan audience.

Elizabeth’s government was nervous about public discussions of succession. The censorship laws meant that plays touching on sensitive political themes had to be disguised. By setting his story in ancient Rome, Shakespeare could explore power, assassination, and political instability without directly criticising the English government. The Roman setting was a protective veil.

Key Fact

Elizabeth I had no heir in 1599. The play’s depiction of political assassination and civil war mirrored genuine English anxieties about what would happen when the queen died. Shakespeare used Rome as a safe setting to explore dangerous political questions about power, legitimacy, and the consequences of removing a leader.

In 1601, just two years after Julius Caesar was first performed, the Earl of Essex launched a failed rebellion against Elizabeth I. Essex’s supporters paid Shakespeare’s company to perform Richard II (a play about the deposition of a king) the night before the uprising, hoping to inspire public support. The incident shows how seriously the Elizabethan government took the power of theatre to influence politics. Julius Caesar’s themes of political assassination and mob manipulation were not abstract — they were live, dangerous topics.

Key Contextual Themes for the Exam

For AQA’s AO3 (context), you need to connect the play to its historical and political background. The most important contextual threads are: the Roman republican ideal that no one man should hold absolute power; the Elizabethan succession crisis and fear of political instability; the divine right debate about whether rulers hold power from God or from the people; and Shakespeare’s use of Plutarch to give historical authority to his drama.

Shakespeare does not give a simple answer to the play’s central question. He presents arguments on both sides — Brutus’s honourable intentions, Cassius’s jealousy, Antony’s grief and political cunning, the mob’s violence. The audience must decide for themselves whether the assassination was justified. This ambiguity is what makes the play so powerful for exam analysis.

title: Chapters 9-10: The Revelations
content_html:
Chapter 9: Dr Lanyon’s Narrative

Stevenson finally delivers the confirmation. Lanyon’s sealed letter is a first-person account of a single terrible night. He receives a desperate note from Jekyll asking him to go to the cabinet and retrieve a drawer of chemicals. At midnight, a “small” stranger calls for the drawer. Lanyon describes him in now-familiar terms: “something abnormal and misbegotten… something seizing, surprising, and revolting.” This is the first time we meet Hyde through Lanyon’s professional, scientific eyes.

Key Fact

Stevenson withholds the transformation until Chapter 9 so that the reveal lands on a scientific, rational character (Lanyon) whom the reader has been taught to trust. The horror is not that Hyde changes — it is that a man of medicine watches it happen.

Hyde drinks the prepared potion. Lanyon describes what follows in stunned clauses: “he reeled, staggered, clutched at the table… and before my eyes — pale and shaken… there stood Henry Jekyll!” The dashes and staccato verbs mimic Lanyon’s shattered narration. Stevenson uses the sentence rhythm to stage the horror in real time.

Lanyon writes: “my life is shaken to its roots; sleep has left me… I cannot, even in my own thoughts, dwell on it without a start of horror.” The knowledge kills him — a direct echo of the Faust story, where the scholar who seeks forbidden knowledge is damned. Stevenson’s warning is moral: some truths are not survivable for those committed to empirical medicine.

Chapter 10: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case

The final chapter is Jekyll’s own long confession. Stevenson shifts voice entirely — the controlled, professional tone of Lanyon gives way to Jekyll’s restless self-examination. Jekyll explains that he was born with “duplicity of life”: a respectable surface and appetites “foreign” to it. He describes his scientific research and the creation of a drug that “could cast off the lower elements” of his personality.

The first transformation brings “incredibly sweet” freedom. As Hyde, Jekyll feels “younger, lighter, happier in body”, and experiences a “solution of the bonds of obligation.” Stevenson is careful: the freedom is pleasurable, which makes the moral warning more interesting. If evil felt only terrible, nobody would pursue it.

Key Fact

Jekyll’s central claim is that ‘man is not truly one, but truly two’. He believed he could separate the good and evil selves — but the evil, given its own body, grows stronger while the good weakens. The drug reveals the truth of duality but cannot manage it.

The Loss of Control

Gradually Jekyll loses the ability to return. After the Carew murder he vows never to take the drug again — but wakes in a park one morning as Hyde without taking it. Stevenson dramatises the addiction: Jekyll’s “powers seemed shaken”, the drug stops working reliably, and the original supply of the salt runs out. What saved him no longer exists. The final transformation is involuntary.

Jekyll’s confession ends with an extraordinary narrative move: he describes his own impending death in present tense. “This, then, is the last time… that Henry Jekyll can think his own thoughts or see his own face… in the glass.” Stevenson uses the last-words framing to make the reader complicit: we are reading a note that ends with the writer’s death.

Late-Victorian Britain was obsessed with doubles: the respectable husband who kept a mistress, the clergyman with a secret life, the civilised man who was also an animal. Stevenson crystallises this fear in one body. The novella was published in 1886, a year of high public tension about hidden vice, and the story became popular immediately. Jekyll’s confession reads like a Victorian nightmare turned inside out: the gentleman does the evil, not a stranger.

Modern criticism often reads Hyde as a figure for repressed Victorian sexuality, addiction, or class anxiety. Stevenson himself called the book ‘a fable’ — inviting interpretation. A strong essay treats the text as open to several readings rather than a puzzle with a single key.

Structure and Effect

Stevenson ends with a written confession because writing is what makes the story survivable. Jekyll’s words are preserved even as he dies; Utterson reads them and gains knowledge that Lanyon could not. The reader is a second Utterson, piecing the evidence into a whole. Structurally, the novella moves from street-level rumour to professional lawyer to scientific eyewitness to the subject’s own pen. Each stage gets closer to the truth — and each stage loses more of the person being described.

Why the Ending Matters

The ending is tragic rather than triumphant. There is no cure, no moral redemption, only a confession. Stevenson refuses the comfort of exorcism: Jekyll dies, Hyde dies, but the double remains as a lesson. The novella closes not with peace but with the reader’s new suspicion — of the doctors, gentlemen and lawyers who seemed so solid in Chapter 1.

title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
content_html:
Key Themes in Journey’s End

Your modern-text essay will always focus on a character, theme, or relationship. Themes run through the entire play, so your essay must range across all three acts — not just one scene. This lesson brings together the play’s major themes and shows you how to structure them into exam-ready arguments. Each theme is supported by key quotations that you should memorise for the closed-book exam.

Heroism and Duty

Sherriff presents heroism not as a grand quality but as the quiet, exhausting act of carrying on. Stanhope is called the best company commander in the battalion, yet he is an alcoholic who can barely function without whisky. Osborne’s heroism lies in his calm decency and willingness to lead the raid despite knowing the danger. Even Trotter is heroic in his own way — his determination to focus on the next meal rather than on fear is a survival strategy that keeps him and others grounded.

The play redefines heroism: it is not the absence of fear, but the decision to continue despite it. Stanhope tells Hibbert that every officer is afraid. The difference between them is not bravery but duty — Stanhope’s sense of duty keeps him at the front even when every instinct tells him to leave. Sherriff asks whether this version of heroism is admirable or simply a form of entrapment imposed by social expectations.

Key Fact

Sherriff redefines heroism as endurance, not glory. Stanhope’s heroism is inseparable from his damage: “It’s the only way to forget.” The play suggests that the real heroism of WWI was not found in dramatic charges but in the daily, grinding act of carrying on when every part of you wants to stop.

Fear and Coping

Every character in the play is afraid, but each copes differently. Stanhope uses alcohol. Osborne uses routine and calm. Trotter uses food and humour. Hibbert tries to escape. Raleigh, at first, does not understand fear because he has not yet experienced the reality of the front. Sherriff uses these contrasting responses to argue that fear is universal — the only question is how you manage it.

The Stanhope–Hibbert confrontation is the play’s most direct exploration of this theme. Stanhope threatens to shoot Hibbert, then admits: “I feel the same — exactly the same.” This moment strips away the idea that courage is a fixed character trait. Instead, Sherriff presents it as a daily choice, made harder by the absence of any support system for psychological damage. The military offered no treatment for what we now call PTSD; the only options were to endure, to drink, or to break.

All the officers in Journey’s End are from the middle or upper-middle class, educated at public schools. Stanhope and Raleigh attended the same school; Osborne was a schoolmaster. The public-school system trained boys for leadership through sport, discipline, and the suppression of emotion. These values — the stiff upper lip, team spirit, duty before self — are both the source of the officers’ strength and the cause of their suffering.

Trotter is the exception: he comes from a lower-middle-class background and is less polished than the others. His promotion to replace Osborne after the raid subtly suggests that the class system is breaking down under the pressure of war — competence matters more than background. The Colonel, meanwhile, represents the upper echelons of the military hierarchy, issuing orders from behind the lines with little regard for the cost to the men who carry them out.

Friendship and Brotherhood

The bonds between the men are the play’s emotional core. Stanhope and Osborne share a deep, unspoken understanding — Osborne is the only person Stanhope trusts. The Stanhope–Raleigh relationship is more complicated: it is built on a school friendship that the war has distorted. Raleigh describes Stanhope as “the one man I could talk to as a friend,” but the Stanhope he finds is a damaged stranger who sees Raleigh as a threat.

Sherriff shows that camaraderie is both the men’s greatest comfort and the source of their greatest pain. Osborne’s death devastates Stanhope precisely because they were close. Stanhope’s tenderness with dying Raleigh shows that the friendship was real all along, but the war made it impossible to express. The play suggests that love and loss in wartime are inseparable.

Futility pervades the play. The raid is carried out at great cost — Osborne dies — to capture a single German prisoner whose information changes nothing. The German attack comes anyway. Raleigh dies. The dugout is destroyed. The play ends without resolution, suggesting that the suffering was meaningless.

Sherriff does not make this argument through speeches or moralising. Instead, he shows it through structure: the play ends where it began, with the sound of shells and the darkness of the dugout. Nothing has been gained. The cycle of duty, fear, loss, and death simply continues. This structural futility mirrors the wider futility of the Western Front, where millions died for gains measured in yards.

Key Fact

The play’s themes work together: heroism is undermined by futility, friendship is destroyed by loss, and the class system that creates leaders also destroys them. The best exam essays explore these connections rather than treating themes in isolation.

Exam Technique — The Modern-Text Essay

A typical modern-text essay question gives you a short quotation from the play and asks you to write an essay. You will often choose one question from two. The question will focus on a character, theme, or relationship. It is a closed-book exam, so you must memorise quotations. Here is a step-by-step approach:

Step 1 — Read the quotation carefully. Identify the character, theme, or idea it relates to. Underline key words in the question.

Step 2 — Plan three to four paragraphs. Each paragraph should make a different point about the question. Aim to cover different parts of the play (not just one act). Each paragraph needs: a point, a quotation (embedded, not bolted on), analysis of language, and a link to context (AO3).

Step 3 — Use the quotation as a springboard. Start your first paragraph by engaging with the given quotation. Analyse its language closely. Then move outwards to other parts of the play.

Step 4 — Embed context into analysis. Do not write a separate “context paragraph.” Instead, weave AO3 into every paragraph: “Stanhope’s reliance on alcohol reflects the widespread use of whisky among officers who had no other support for what we now recognise as PTSD.”

Step 5 — Conclude briefly. Sum up your argument in two to three sentences. Do not introduce new evidence.

The assessment objectives for the modern-text essay typically include: AO1 — your response to the text, supported by quotations and references; AO3 — understanding of context (historical, social, cultural); and AO4 — spelling, punctuation, and grammar alongside accurate use of literary terminology. Allow roughly 45–50 minutes for this question. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact mark allocation and the balance between AOs.

title: The Creature's Story
content_html:
The Creature’s Narrative

Chapters 11–16 give the Creature its own voice — the innermost layer of the nested narrative. The Creature tells Victor how it wandered alone after being abandoned, confused by its senses: “A strange multiplicity of sensations seized me, and I saw, felt, heard, and smelt at the same time.” Shelley presents the Creature as experiencing the world like a newborn — overwhelmed, vulnerable, and without any frame of reference. This is her most powerful argument for the Creature’s essential innocence.

The Creature discovers fire and is burned, learns that humans flee from its appearance, and eventually finds shelter in a hovel attached to the cottage of the De Lacey family. It watches them through a crack in the wall, learning language, emotion, and human relationships. Felix teaches Safie (a Turkish woman) to read using Volney’s Ruins of Empires, and the Creature learns alongside her — absorbing knowledge of human history, injustice, and civilisation.

Key Fact

From the De Laceys, the Creature learns: (1) language — giving it the ability to express its suffering and desire for connection; (2) emotion — it feels joy watching the family’s love and weeps at their hardships; (3) self-awareness — it sees its own reflection and realises it is “hideously deformed.” Education gives the Creature the tools to understand its suffering but not the power to escape it.

The Three Books

The Creature finds three books that shape its understanding: Paradise Lost by Milton, Plutarch’s Lives, and The Sorrows of Young Werther by Goethe. Paradise Lost is the most significant. The Creature reads it as “a true history” and identifies with both Adam and Satan. Like Adam, it was created by a “creator” who should have cared for it. Like Satan, it has been cast out and now burns with rejection and rage. The Creature asks: “Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay to mould me man?” — quoting Milton’s Adam directly.

This allusion is central to the novel. Like Adam, the Creature did not ask to be made. Like Satan, it has been rejected by its creator and now seeks revenge. Shelley asks the reader: if God abandoned Adam, would Adam be justified in turning to evil? The Creature’s identification with both figures creates deep moral ambiguity — it is simultaneously sympathetic (abandoned child) and terrifying (vengeful outcast).

The Creature’s plan is careful and rational. It approaches old De Lacey when the rest of the family is away, knowing the blind man cannot judge it by appearance. The conversation is moving: De Lacey responds with kindness, calling the Creature “friend.” For a brief moment, genuine human connection seems possible. But when Felix, Agatha, and Safie return, they see the Creature and react with horror and violence. Felix beats it with a stick. The family abandons their cottage the next day. The one chance for acceptance is destroyed by visual prejudice.

The Birth of Rage

After the De Lacey rejection, the Creature describes a fundamental shift: “From that moment I declared everlasting war against the species.” The word “everlasting” and the phrase “declared war” mark a transformation from victim to aggressor. Shelley does not excuse the Creature’s subsequent violence, but she makes clear what caused it: systematic, universal rejection based on appearance alone. The Creature tried kindness, reason, and patience. Every attempt was met with horror and violence. Shelley’s argument is disturbing: society’s refusal to see beyond surface appearance creates the very monsters it fears.

The Creature also finds Victor’s journal and learns the full horror of its creation: that Victor was disgusted by it from the moment of its birth. It discovers it was made from dead body parts and that its creator considered it an abomination. This knowledge — that it was never loved, never even tolerated — completes the Creature’s transformation. It heads for Geneva to confront Victor, fuelled by a mixture of grief and rage.

Key Fact

“From that moment I declared everlasting war against the species” marks the Creature’s turning point. It is not born violent — it is made violent by: (1) Victor’s abandonment at creation, (2) universal human rejection based on its appearance, (3) the De Lacey family’s violent response to its attempt at friendship, and (4) discovering Victor’s journal, which reveals it was always considered an abomination. Shelley argues that monstrosity is created by society, not by nature.

The Creature’s story is Shelley’s strongest statement on the nature versus nurture debate. The Creature begins with the capacity for love, compassion, and learning. It weeps at the De Laceys’ suffering, saves a drowning girl, and gathers firewood for the cottage family. Every instinct is generous. It is only after repeated, universal rejection that it turns to violence. Shelley, influenced by Rousseau, argues that humans (and human-like beings) are made good or evil by their treatment, not by their inherent nature. Victor’s failure to nurture his creation is the root cause of all the novel’s tragedies.

title: Act 2: Duncan's Murder & Guilt
content_html:
The Dagger Soliloquy (Act 2, Scene 1)

As Macbeth prepares to murder Duncan, he hallucinates a floating dagger: “Is this a dagger which I see before me, / The handle toward my hand?” The dagger’s handle points toward him, as if inviting him to grasp it — suggesting that the murder is being offered to him rather than forced upon him. This raises the central question: is the dagger a supernatural apparition sent by the witches, or a projection of Macbeth’s own guilt-ridden imagination?

Macbeth tries to seize the dagger: “Come, let me clutch thee. / I have thee not, and yet I see thee still.” The gap between seeing and touching — between desire and reality — mirrors the gap between appearance and reality that runs through the play. As the soliloquy progresses, the dagger becomes covered in “gouts of blood” — a vision of the murder’s aftermath before it has even happened. Shakespeare uses the hallucination to show that Macbeth’s mind is already consumed by guilt before the act itself.

Key Fact

The dagger soliloquy (Act 2, Scene 1) shows Macbeth hallucinating a blood-covered dagger pointing toward Duncan’s chamber. It is deliberately ambiguous: the dagger could be a supernatural sign (sent by the witches) or a hallucination born of Macbeth’s own tortured conscience. Either reading supports the play’s themes.

Blood and Water — The Central Motif

After the murder, Shakespeare uses blood to explore the Macbeths’ contrasting reactions. Macbeth stares at his hands: “This is a sorry sight.” Lady Macbeth dismisses him: “A foolish thought, to say a sorry sight.” She views emotional responses as weakness. But blood on their hands becomes the play’s most important symbol.

Macbeth’s despair peaks with: “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand? No, this my hand will rather / The multitudinous seas incarnadine, / Making the green one red.” The hyperbole is extraordinary: rather than the ocean cleaning his hands, his guilt would turn the entire sea red. The shift from the Latinate “incardnadine” to the blunt Anglo-Saxon “making the green one red” mirrors how horror strips away Macbeth’s eloquence.

Lady Macbeth returns from planting the daggers: “My hands are of your colour; but I shame / To wear a heart so white.” “Your colour” = red (guilt); “heart so white” = cowardice. She shames Macbeth while claiming equal guilt but superior composure.

She declares: “A little water clears us of this deed.” This line is devastatingly ironic. She believes physical washing removes moral guilt. This foreshadowing is among the play’s most powerful: in Act 5, the sleepwalking Lady Macbeth cries “Out, damned spot!” and “All the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand.” The woman who dismissed guilt easily is destroyed by it.

The Porter Scene (Act 2, Scene 3)

The Porter, drunk from celebrations, imagines himself as gatekeeper of Hell: “Here’s a knocking indeed! If a man were porter of hell-gate, he should have old turning the key.” This metaphor is deeply appropriate — Macbeth’s castle has literally become Hell. The Porter imagines admitting three sinners: a farmer who hoarded grain (self-interest), an equivocator who committed treason (deception), and a tailor who stole cloth (theft). Each mirrors Macbeth’s crimes.

The constant knocking symbolises fate approaching. Macduff — the man who will eventually kill Macbeth — waits on the other side. The knocking is persistent and unavoidable, just as Macbeth’s punishment is inevitable.

Key Fact

The Porter’s three sinners — a greedy farmer, a treasonous equivocator, and a thieving tailor — each mirror Macbeth’s crimes: self-interest, deception, and theft of the crown. The knocking at the gate symbolises fate (Macduff) approaching, and the castle-as-Hell metaphor shows that regicide has transformed Macbeth’s home into a place of damnation.

The Discovery and Reactions

Macduff discovers Duncan’s body with visceral horror: “O horror, horror, horror! / Tongue nor heart cannot conceive nor name thee!” The triple repetition may echo the Holy Trinity, suggesting the murder offends God. Macbeth performs grief: “His silver skin laced with his golden blood” — precious colours emphasise Duncan’s royalty, but the elaborate language feels rehearsed. Donalbain’s “There’s daggers in men’s smiles” captures the theme of duplicity perfectly.

Immediately after the murder, Macbeth hears a voice cry: “Methought I heard a voice cry, ‘Sleep no more! / Macbeth does murder sleep.’” Sleep represents innocence, peace, and the natural order. By killing Duncan (who was sleeping), Macbeth has murdered sleep itself — he has destroyed his own capacity for rest and peace. Shakespeare personifies sleep as “innocent sleep, / Sleep that knits up the ravelled sleave of care” — a healing, restorative force that Macbeth can never access again.

He also cannot say “Amen” when the guards cry out in their sleep: “I could not say ‘Amen’ / When they did say ‘God bless us.’” This shows Macbeth is spiritually cut off from God. A Jacobean audience would understand this as proof that regicide brings not just political chaos but spiritual damnation.

title: Context: Post-War Anxieties
content_html:
Golding and the Second World War

William Golding served in the Royal Navy during the Second World War. He commanded a rocket-launching ship on D-Day and witnessed the liberation of concentration camps. These experiences destroyed any lingering belief he had in human goodness. He later wrote: ‘I began to see what people were capable of doing’. This personal disillusionment is the engine of Lord of the Flies (1954) — a novel that insists civilisation is a thin veneer, and that savagery lives inside every human being, including children.

Golding was also a schoolteacher at Bishop Wordsworth’s School in Salisbury. He observed how quickly groups of boys could descend into cruelty when left unsupervised. The novel draws directly on these observations: the boys on the island are not fictional abstractions but reflections of real behaviour Golding witnessed in classrooms and playgrounds.

Key Fact

Golding’s wartime service — D-Day, witnessing concentration camp liberation, and observing schoolboys’ behaviour — convinced him that evil is innate in human nature, not caused by society. This belief drives every chapter of Lord of the Flies.

Cold War Anxieties and the Nuclear Backdrop

The novel is set during an unspecified nuclear war. In Chapter 1, Piggy refers to ‘the atom bomb’ and says that ‘they’re all dead’, meaning the adults. The boys’ plane was evacuating them from England when it was shot down. The Cold War backdrop is crucial: in the 1950s, nuclear annihilation felt like a genuine possibility. Golding places children — symbols of innocence — into a world that adults have already destroyed through exactly the kind of violence the boys will replicate on the island.

The dead parachutist who lands on the mountain in Chapter 6, mistaken for ‘the beast’, is a literal remnant of the adult war above. His presence connects the boys’ descent into savagery with the civilised world’s descent into nuclear conflict. Golding’s point is devastating: the adults are no better than the children. The naval officer who ‘rescues’ them at the end arrives on a warship, about to participate in the very same violence.

The naval officer is ‘moved and a little embarrassed’ by the boys’ savagery, then turns to face his own warship — a cruiser armed with weapons of mass destruction. Golding forces the reader to see that the officer has no moral authority. The ‘rescue’ is an illusion: the boys are simply being returned to a world that is itself at war.

Subverting The Coral Island

Lord of the Flies is a deliberate response to R.M. Ballantyne’s The Coral Island (1858), a Victorian adventure novel in which three boys — Ralph, Jack, and Peterkin — are stranded on a tropical island and thrive through courage, teamwork, and Christian morality. Golding borrows the names Ralph and Jack but reverses the outcome entirely. Where Ballantyne’s boys conquer nature and remain civilised, Golding’s boys destroy each other.

Ballantyne’s novel reflects Victorian confidence in British superiority and the civilising mission of the Empire. Golding — writing after two world wars, the Holocaust, and the invention of the atomic bomb — found this optimism absurd. Ralph references The Coral Island directly in Chapter 2: ‘It’s like in a book… Treasure Island… Coral Island’. This optimism is quickly destroyed.

Key Fact

Golding deliberately uses the names Ralph and Jack from The Coral Island to set up expectations of a cheerful adventure — then systematically destroys them. Where Ballantyne’s boys stay civilised, Golding’s descend into murder, showing that Victorian optimism about human nature was a dangerous fantasy.

Original Sin and the Nature of Evil

Golding was deeply influenced by the Christian concept of original sin — the idea that humans are born with an innate capacity for evil. The island echoes the Garden of Eden: a beautiful, bountiful paradise that the boys corrupt through moral failure. Simon’s encounter with the Lord of the Flies in Chapter 8 functions as a temptation scene, where the beast tells him: ‘Fancy thinking the Beast was something you could hunt and kill!’ The beast is not external; it is inside every boy.

The philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau argued that humans are born good and that society corrupts them (the noble savage theory). Golding’s novel is a direct rejection of this idea. By placing boys in nature without adult society, he tests Rousseau’s theory — and it fails spectacularly. Without civilisation’s constraints, the boys descend into tribal violence. Golding sides with Thomas Hobbes, who argued that without authority, life would be ‘solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short’.

title: Act 2: Tensions & the Raid
content_html:
Act 2 — The Pressure Builds

Act 2 of Journey’s End deepens the tensions established in Act 1. The German attack is now imminent, and the Colonel arrives with orders for a dangerous trench raid. Stanhope must send men across no man’s land to capture a German prisoner for intelligence. This act also contains two of the play’s most important scenes: Stanhope’s decision to censor Raleigh’s letter, and Hibbert’s attempt to leave the front line by claiming illness.

Sherriff structures Act 2 around the theme of duty versus self-preservation. Every character is forced to choose between obeying orders and protecting themselves or the people they care about. The raid hangs over the act like a sentence of death, and the audience watches the men respond in different ways: Osborne with quiet acceptance, Stanhope with fierce control, Hibbert with desperate evasion, and Raleigh with naïve willingness.

Key Fact

The Colonel orders the raid to capture a German soldier for intelligence about the expected attack. Stanhope objects to sending Osborne on such a dangerous mission, but the Colonel insists. This reveals the military hierarchy’s disregard for individual lives — decisions made from behind the lines directly cause the deaths of men the audience has come to care about.

The Censorship Scene

One of Act 2’s most revealing scenes occurs when Stanhope insists on reading Raleigh’s letter home before it is sent. He has been dreading this moment — convinced that Raleigh will describe his censorship of his own letters was a real practice during WWI, and Sherriff uses it here to create dramatic irony.

When Osborne reads the letter aloud, it contains nothing but admiration: Raleigh describes Stanhope as “the best company commander in the battalion” and says how proud he is to serve under him. Stanhope is stunned and ashamed. The moment is devastating because it reveals the gap between Stanhope’s tortured self-image and how others actually see him. He has been so consumed by guilt and fear that he cannot recognise loyalty when it is offered.

Stanhope’s insistence on censoring the letter exposes his deepest fear: not the Germans, not death, but being seen as he truly is. His identity is split between the heroic schoolboy Raleigh remembers and the alcoholic wreck he believes himself to be. The dramatic irony is powerful — the audience already suspects that Raleigh’s letter will be positive, but Stanhope cannot imagine it. His shame has so distorted his perception that he is incapable of trusting anyone’s good opinion of him.

After hearing the letter, Stanhope quietly says he will not censor it after all. This small moment of grace is one of the few times in the play where Stanhope lets his guard down. Sherriff shows that beneath the toughness, Stanhope is still capable of being moved — but the war has made vulnerability feel like a threat.

Hibbert’s Attempt to Leave

Second Lieutenant Hibbert claims he has neuralgia (severe headaches) and asks to be sent to the rear. Stanhope sees through the excuse immediately and confronts Hibbert in one of the play’s most intense scenes. He tells Hibbert that every officer is afraid — including himself — and threatens to shoot him if he tries to leave.

This scene is crucial because it shows Stanhope at his most complex. He is simultaneously cruel (threatening to shoot a fellow officer) and honest (admitting his own fear). When he says that he, too, has considered pretending to be ill, he strips away the mask of the fearless leader. The scene also raises an uncomfortable moral question: is Hibbert a coward, or simply a man who has reached his breaking point? Sherriff refuses to give a simple answer. Hibbert’s fear is real, even if his excuse is not.

Key Fact

Stanhope tells Hibbert: “If you went — Loss of Raleigh’s map will be — irreplaceable.” He threatens to shoot Hibbert if he leaves, but then admits his own terror. The scene ends with both men agreeing to go on together. Sherriff shows that courage is not the absence of fear but the decision to carry on despite it.

The Raid Preparations

The Colonel selects Osborne and Raleigh to lead the raiding party. Stanhope objects, not wanting to risk Osborne, but the Colonel dismisses his concerns. This moment reveals the callousness of military command: the Colonel is more interested in capturing a prisoner than in the lives of the men he sends. He offers Osborne a box of cigars as a reward, a detail that highlights the grotesque disparity between the commanders behind the lines and the men who face death.

The night before the raid, Osborne and Raleigh sit together in the dugout. Osborne reads aloud from Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, and they talk about England, home, and mundane things. This quiet domestic scene, set against the knowledge that one or both may die tomorrow, is one of Sherriff’s most effective dramatic techniques. The contrast between the ordinariness of their conversation and the horror of what awaits them creates unbearable tension.

Osborne’s choice of reading material is significant. Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland is a children’s book about a nonsensical world where normal rules do not apply. There is a clear parallel with the war: the officers have fallen into their own nightmarish wonderland where death is random and authority makes no sense. The book also connects to Osborne’s former life as a schoolmaster — it is a reminder of the civilised, orderly world he has left behind.

By having Osborne read a children’s book just before he goes to his death, Sherriff emphasises his innocence and gentleness. It also functions as a form of escape: Osborne retreats into a fantasy world rather than facing the reality of the next day. The scene is profoundly moving because it shows a good man quietly preparing to die.

Themes in Act 2

Act 2 brings several key themes into sharp focus. The conflict between duty and self-preservation is dramatised through Hibbert. The gap between the military command and the men on the ground is shown through the Colonel’s casual ordering of the raid. The theme of appearance versus reality deepens as Stanhope’s fear is contrasted with his outward authority, and Raleigh’s admiring letter reveals the disconnect between Stanhope’s self-image and how he is perceived. Every scene in Act 2 tightens the pressure towards the inevitable catastrophe of the raid.

title: Context: Victorian Duality
content_html:
The Victorian World of Jekyll and Hyde

Robert Louis Stevenson published The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde in 1886, during the height of the Victorian era. The novella was an immediate sensation — 40,000 copies sold in the first six months. It struck a nerve because it exposed something Victorians desperately wanted to hide: the idea that respectable, civilised people harboured dark and violent desires beneath the surface.

Victorian society placed enormous value on respectability. A gentleman was expected to be rational, moral, restrained, and publicly virtuous. Yet behind the polished facades of London’s townhouses, many wealthy men led secret double lives — visiting opium dens, engaging in illicit relationships, and indulging desires they publicly condemned. Stevenson’s novella tore away this mask of respectability and forced his readers to confront their own hypocrisy.

Key Fact

Victorian gentlemen were expected to suppress all immoral urges. Jekyll creates Hyde not because he is unusually evil, but because the pressure to appear respectable is unbearable. Stevenson suggests that all humans have a dual nature — the Victorians simply refused to admit it.

Repression and the Double Life

The theme of repression runs through every page of the novella. Jekyll confesses in his final statement that he “learned to recognise the thorough and primitive duality of man.” He understood that every person contains both good and evil impulses. The problem was not the impulses themselves, but Victorian society’s insistence that they did not exist.

Jekyll’s transformation is not about gaining new evil qualities — it is about releasing desires he already possessed. He admits: “the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde.” This early confidence reveals his fatal flaw: the belief that he can control the darkness within. Stevenson uses Jekyll’s gradual loss of control to warn that repression is not a solution — it only makes the eventual release of those desires more violent and destructive.

Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, just twenty-seven years before Stevenson’s novella. Darwin’s theory of evolution argued that humans had evolved from more primitive creatures. This horrified many Victorians because it suggested that beneath the veneer of civilisation, humans were still animals — capable of savage, instinctive violence. Hyde is repeatedly described in animalistic terms: he has “ape-like fury,” he is compared to a “troglodyte,” and witnesses describe something inhuman about his appearance. Stevenson draws on evolutionary anxiety to suggest that Hyde represents the primitive, pre-civilised self that lurks within every person.

The science versus religion debate was at its height. Many Victorians feared that if Darwin was right and humans were merely evolved animals, then morality itself had no divine foundation. Jekyll’s experiment — using science to separate good from evil — reflects this anxiety. His failure suggests that good and evil cannot be neatly divided, and that attempting to do so through science leads to catastrophe.

The Gothic Genre

Stevenson’s novella belongs to the Gothic tradition. Gothic literature explored the dark side of human nature, featuring supernatural events, psychological terror, and settings that reflected inner turmoil. Earlier Gothic novels like Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein (1818) and Bram Stoker’s Dracula (1897) shared similar concerns about science overreaching its boundaries and the beast within civilised humanity.

Victorian Gothic moved the horror from remote castles into the heart of London. Stevenson’s fog-choked streets, sinister doorways, and respectable houses hiding terrible secrets reflect the idea that evil is not somewhere far away — it lives next door. The novella’s famous description, “The fog still slept on the wing above the drowned city,” turns London itself into a Gothic landscape where nothing is quite what it seems.

Key Fact

Victorian Gothic fiction brought horror into everyday urban settings. Stevenson uses London’s fog, gas-lit streets, and locked doors to create a world where respectability and monstrosity exist side by side. The Gothic setting mirrors the novella’s central theme: that darkness hides within the familiar.

Urban London and Social Division

The London of Jekyll and Hyde is a city of sharp contrasts. Wealthy areas like Cavendish Square sit close to dangerous, poverty-stricken slums like Soho. Jekyll’s grand house has a front entrance on a respectable street and a back entrance through a sinister, blistered door in a dingy lane. This physical layout mirrors the novella’s central metaphor: the respectable exterior and the hidden, shameful interior.

Stevenson grew up in Edinburgh, a city famously divided between the respectable New Town and the crime-ridden Old Town. He was the son of a devoutly religious lighthouse engineer but rebelled against his upbringing, exploring Edinburgh’s seedy underworld as a young man. He was also influenced by the real case of Deacon Brodie — an eighteenth-century Edinburgh cabinet-maker who was a respected citizen by day and a burglar by night. Brodie was eventually caught and hanged. Stevenson had a cabinet made by Brodie in his childhood bedroom, and later wrote a play about him. The duality of Jekyll and Hyde has its roots in Stevenson’s own city and personal experience.

The Edexcel Exam: What You Need to Know

For Edexcel 1ET0 Component 2, Section A, you will answer a two-part question on Jekyll and Hyde. Part (a) asks you to analyse an extract of around 400 words, focusing on language and how Stevenson creates meaning (AO1 + AO2). Part (b) asks you to explore a theme, character, or idea across the whole novella (AO1 + AO2). This is a closed book exam, so you must memorise key quotations. Context is not separately assessed, but strong responses weave contextual understanding into their analysis naturally.
