title: Character Analysis
content_html:
Victor Frankenstein: Creator and Destroyer

Victor is the novel’s central figure, but Shelley makes him deeply problematic. He is brilliant, passionate, and capable of great devotion — yet he is also selfish, secretive, and morally paralysed when it matters most. His defining characteristic is hubris: the belief that he can play God by creating life. He imagines “a new species would bless me as its creator and source,” revealing that his ambition is driven by a desire for glory, not by compassion or curiosity.

Victor’s tragedy is that he has genuine insight but cannot act on it. He warns Walton that the “acquirement of knowledge” is dangerous, yet in the same breath suggests another “may succeed.” He calls himself the “true murderer” of William and Justine, yet never confesses. He promises the Creature a companion, then destroys it. Shelley presents Victor as a man whose self-awareness is always one step behind his actions — he understands what he has done wrong only after it is too late.

Key Fact

Victor is not simply evil — he is morally weak. His failures are failures of responsibility: he creates without planning, abandons without remorse, and stays silent when speaking could save lives. Shelley asks whether a man who does terrible things through negligence and cowardice is more dangerous than one who acts with deliberate malice.

The Creature: Monster or Victim?

The Creature is the novel’s most complex character. Born innocent, it learns language, develops empathy, and seeks connection. It secretly helps the De Laceys, restrains itself when attacked by Felix, and approaches the blind father with eloquent humility. Yet it also murders William, frames Justine, kills Clerval, and strangles Elizabeth. Shelley refuses to let the reader settle on a simple judgment: the Creature is simultaneously sympathetic and terrifying.

The key to understanding the Creature is the quotation “I am malicious because I am miserable.” Its violence is not innate but caused by universal rejection. The Creature’s identification with Satan from Paradise Lost — “I ought to be thy Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel” — frames it as a being unjustly cast out by its creator. Shelley uses the Creature to challenge the reader’s assumptions about monstrosity: is the real monster the being who looks horrifying, or the man who created it and walked away?

The Creature speaks more eloquently than any other character in the novel. Its language is rich, rhetorical, and deeply literary, shaped by its reading of Paradise Lost, Plutarch, and Goethe. This creates a powerful contrast with its physical appearance. When the Creature declares “Beware; for I am fearless, and therefore powerful,” the syntax is controlled and the logic is sharp. When it cries “I, the miserable and the abandoned, am an abortion,” the rhythm is almost poetic. Shelley uses the Creature’s eloquence to force the reader to listen to it, even when its actions are horrifying. If it spoke in grunts, we could dismiss it as a monster. Because it speaks like Milton’s Satan, we must engage with its argument.

Robert Walton: The Reader’s Surrogate

Walton mirrors Victor in ambition and isolation but ultimately makes a different choice. His letters to Margaret reveal a man who “would sacrifice my fortune, my existence, my every hope” for discovery — language that directly echoes Victor’s obsession. Yet when his crew demand he turn back, Walton listens. He chooses the lives of others over his own glory. Shelley uses Walton as the novel’s moral benchmark — proof that ambition can be tempered by responsibility. He represents the reader: someone who hears Victor’s cautionary tale and must decide whether to learn from it.

Elizabeth Lavenza: The Silent Victim

Elizabeth is Victor’s adopted sister and later his wife. She is presented as beautiful, gentle, and morally courageous — she alone speaks in Justine’s defence at the trial. Yet Shelley also makes Elizabeth conspicuously passive. She waits for Victor throughout the novel, writing letters that go unanswered, trusting him despite his obvious secrecy. Her murder on the wedding night is a consequence of Victor’s actions, not her own. Modern readers often note that Elizabeth functions less as a fully developed character and more as a symbol of what Victor stands to lose — and what the Creature is denied.

Key Fact

Elizabeth is the novel’s moral voice during Justine’s trial, but she is also its most powerless figure. She cannot protect herself because Victor keeps her ignorant of the danger. Her murder is the direct result of Victor’s secrecy and the destruction of the female creature. Shelley uses Elizabeth to show how Victor’s failures harm not just himself but everyone around him.

Henry Clerval and the De Laceys

Henry Clerval is Victor’s best friend and his polar opposite. Where Victor is consumed by science, Clerval loves literature, languages, and human company. He nurses Victor through his breakdown, asks no intrusive questions, and brings warmth wherever he goes. His murder by the Creature is deeply significant: Victor’s failure to warn Clerval about the danger directly costs Clerval his life. Clerval represents the human warmth that Victor sacrificed for ambition.

The De Lacey family serves a dual purpose: they educate the Creature and then reject it. The blind father’s brief acceptance proves the Creature is capable of forming human connections — only its appearance prevents this. Felix’s violent reaction shows that even kind, moral people judge by appearance. The De Laceys are themselves victims of injustice (exiled for helping a wrongly accused man), which makes their rejection of the Creature even more painful. Shelley shows that prejudice is universal, even among the virtuous.

Justine Moritz is a servant in the Frankenstein household who is wrongly convicted of William’s murder. She makes a false confession under pressure from her confessor, demonstrating how institutional power (the Church) can override truth. Victor knows she is innocent but stays silent. Justine’s execution is Shelley’s critique of a justice system that punishes the powerless based on circumstantial evidence. Like the Creature, Justine is judged by something beyond her control — the evidence planted against her, just as the Creature is judged by its appearance.

Justine’s name itself is significant: it derives from the Latin justitia, meaning justice. Her wrongful execution is an act of profound injustice, making her name bitterly ironic. Shelley uses Justine to show that the legal system, like individual humans, can be cruel to those it should protect.

title: Character Analysis
content_html:
Leon: Resilience and Loyalty

Leon is nine years old, mixed-race, and the novel’s focaliser. Everything the reader knows is filtered through his understanding. He is defined by two qualities above all: fierce loyalty to Jake, and extraordinary resilience in the face of a system that repeatedly fails him.

Key Fact

Leon’s loyalty and resilience exist in tension. His loyalty drives him to fight for Jake — which the system labels as ‘difficult behaviour.’ His resilience allows him to survive, but surviving means gradually accepting a life without his brother. De Waal shows that the qualities the system punishes (determination, anger) are the same qualities keeping Leon alive.

Leon’s naïveté is crucial to De Waal’s method. He does not understand racism, class, mental illness, or institutional failure as concepts. He simply experiences their effects. This makes him a powerful vehicle for social criticism because the reader can see what Leon cannot, creating both empathy and outrage.

Part 1: Leon is a protector — defined entirely by his relationship to Jake and Carol. He is capable, resourceful, and unnervingly adult in his caring responsibilities.

Part 2: Separated from Jake, Leon struggles with identity. His behaviour deteriorates as grief and anger find no productive outlet. He oscillates between accepting Maureen’s love and rejecting it out of guilt.

Part 3: Leon becomes more defiant and purposeful. His quest for Jake gives him direction. During the riots, he experiences a fusion of personal and political anger that matures his understanding. By the ending, he has not ‘healed’ — but he has survived, which is itself an act of resistance.

Jake: Innocence and Loss

Jake is a baby — he has no voice, no agency, and no understanding of what is happening to him. He functions in the novel primarily as an emblem of what Leon is fighting to keep. Jake represents innocence, family, and everything the system takes from Leon.

Crucially, Jake’s whiteness makes him visible to the system in ways Leon is not. He is adopted by a middle-class family who can provide material comfort but not the sibling bond that Leon offers. De Waal uses Jake to expose the care system’s racial hierarchy: a white baby is a ‘success story’ for adoption statistics, while a mixed-race older child is a ‘difficult placement.’

Carol: Failed by Everyone

Carol is Leon and Jake’s mother. She is white, working-class, and struggling with mental health problems and substance issues. De Waal refuses to demonise her. Carol is not a bad mother — she is a woman without support, without resources, and without adequate mental health services. Her decline is the result of systemic failure, not personal wickedness.

Key Fact

De Waal presents Carol through Leon’s eyes — and Leon loves her. He remembers good times, moments of affection, her smell. This prevents the reader from writing Carol off as simply ‘a bad parent.’ The novel asks: who failed Carol? Where were the services, the community, the father figures?

Carol connects to themes of class, poverty, and gender. She is a single mother in Thatcher’s Britain, where welfare services are being cut. Her absent partners (both Leon’s father and Jake’s) face no consequences, while Carol bears all the responsibility and all the blame.

De Waal uses Carol to critique a system that punishes mothers for poverty rather than providing support. The care system intervenes to remove children but does nothing to address the causes of Carol’s collapse — her isolation, her untreated illness, her lack of financial stability.

Maureen: The Foster Mother

Maureen is Jamaican-British, warm, patient, and experienced. She represents an alternative model of care — community-based, culturally aware, and rooted in love rather than procedure. Her home is sensory: food, music, colour, conversation. She provides Leon with stability, cultural identity, and the first genuine safety he has known.

However, Maureen is not idealised. She has limitations — she cannot reunite Leon with Jake, she cannot undo his trauma, and she must navigate the same institutional system that failed him. De Waal uses Maureen to show that individual love, however powerful, cannot compensate for systemic injustice.

Tina: The Social Worker

Tina represents the institutional system. She is not cruel — she is overworked, bound by policy, and making decisions within a framework that was never designed to serve children like Leon. De Waal presents Tina with nuance — she cares, but her caring is constrained by caseloads, budgets, and rules she did not create.

Tina’s language is significant: she uses euphemisms and bureaucratic terms that obscure what is really happening. “Permanency planning” means Leon will never go home. “Contact arrangements” means limited, supervised visits that will eventually stop. De Waal shows how institutional language can be a form of violence — removing clarity from children who deserve honesty.

title: Chapters 1-4: Mystery & Terror
content_html:
Chapter 1: The Door and Enfield’s Story

The novella opens with two respectable gentlemen, Mr Utterson (a lawyer) and his kinsman Mr Enfield, walking through London. They pass a sinister door on a rundown street, and Enfield tells a strange story: he once witnessed a man “calmly trampl[e] over a child’s body” at a street corner. The man was Hyde. The crowd surrounded him, and Hyde paid compensation through a cheque signed by the respectable Dr Jekyll. Enfield’s reaction to Hyde is visceral: “I had taken a loathing to my gentleman at first sight.”

Stevenson uses mystery as his primary structural device. The reader, like Utterson, is given pieces of a puzzle without the full picture. We know Hyde is connected to Jekyll but not how. We know the door leads to Jekyll’s laboratory but not why Hyde uses it. The first four chapters build a web of second-hand narration: Enfield tells Utterson, Utterson investigates, but nobody speaks to Jekyll directly. This narrative structure mirrors the Victorian culture of secrecy — gentlemen do not ask uncomfortable questions.

Key Fact

Hyde tramples a young girl “calmly” — without remorse or hesitation. The word “calmly” is crucial: it shows that Hyde’s violence is not passionate rage but cold indifference to human suffering. He treats the child as though she does not exist. This establishes Hyde as a figure without empathy or conscience — the purely selfish part of human nature unleashed.

Chapter 2: Utterson’s Investigation

Utterson reads Jekyll’s will and discovers that everything is left to Hyde — including the provision that if Jekyll “disappears for any period exceeding three calendar months,” Hyde inherits. This alarming clause suggests either blackmail or something worse. Utterson visits Dr Lanyon, Jekyll’s old friend, who dismisses Jekyll’s recent scientific work as “unscientific balderdash.” The disagreement between the two doctors hints that Jekyll has crossed a moral boundary that Lanyon refuses to follow.

Utterson stakes out the sinister door and finally meets Hyde. His reaction is the same indefinable revulsion that every character experiences: “Mr Hyde was pale and dwarfish, he gave an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation.” Hyde produces a “disgusting” impression that Utterson cannot explain: “God bless me, the man seems hardly human! Something troglodytic.” The word troglodytic links Hyde to prehistoric humanity, reinforcing the degeneration theme.

Notice that characters consistently cannot describe what is wrong with Hyde. This is Stevenson’s deliberate technique: by making Hyde’s evil indefinable, he makes it universal. Hyde does not look like a specific type of villain — he embodies a feeling of wrongness that everyone recognises but nobody can articulate. In the exam, this is a powerful AO2 point about Stevenson’s language choices.

Chapter 3: Jekyll’s Reassurance

Utterson confronts Jekyll, who dismisses his concerns: “I can be rid of Mr Hyde… whenever I choose.” This is deeply ironic because the reader later learns that Jekyll is already losing control. Jekyll’s confidence is the confidence of an addict who believes he can stop at any time. Stevenson uses proleptic irony throughout: statements that seem reassuring on first reading become ominous once the truth is revealed.

Chapter 4: The Carew Murder

Hyde’s violence escalates dramatically. He murders Sir Danvers Carew, a respected MP, in a frenzied attack witnessed by a maidservant: “Mr Hyde broke out of all bounds and clubbed him to the earth. And next moment, with ape-like fury, he was trampling his victim underfoot and hailing down a storm of blows, under which the bones were audibly shattering.” The language is extraordinarily violent: “ape-like fury,” “trampling,” “bones audibly shattering.” Stevenson moves from the cold trampling of a child to a savage murder, showing Hyde’s escalating loss of control.

Carew is described as “an aged beautiful gentleman with white hair” who approaches Hyde “with a very pretty manner of politeness.” The contrast between Carew’s gentleness and Hyde’s savagery is absolute. Carew represents everything that Victorian respectability values: age, beauty, courtesy, and public service. Hyde’s destruction of him symbolises the assault of the primitive, selfish self on civilised values.

The maidservant who witnesses the murder does so by moonlight — she is at an upstairs window, looking down. This vertical perspective (observer above, crime below) mirrors the structure of Jekyll’s house and Victorian society itself: respectability lives upstairs, while violence happens in the streets below.

Key Fact

The Carew murder is described with escalating violence: “with ape-like fury, he was trampling his victim underfoot and hailing down a storm of blows, under which the bones were audibly shattering.” “Ape-like” links to degeneration, “trampling” echoes the child incident (showing escalation), and “bones audibly shattering” uses sound imagery to make the violence disturbingly real.

title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
content_html:
Theme: Independence and Self-Respect

The novel’s central theme is Jane’s fight for independence in a world that denies it to women, the poor, and the powerless. Every stage of Jane’s journey tests her self-respect: at Gateshead she defies Mrs Reed, at Lowood she endures Brocklehurst, at Thornfield she demands equality, and at Moor House she refuses to surrender to St John. Her final choice to return to Rochester is an act of freedom, not submission — she comes with her own money, her own will, and her own terms.

“I care for myself” is the novel’s moral compass. It does not mean selfishness — it means that integrity cannot be sacrificed for love, comfort, or duty. Jane’s self-respect is the foundation on which every other relationship is built. Without it, love becomes dependence; with it, love becomes partnership.

Key Fact

Independence is tested at every location: Gateshead (defiance), Lowood (endurance), Thornfield (equality), Moor House (refusal of duty without love), Ferndean (return as equal). The novel argues that true love is only possible between independent people — dependence corrupts relationship into ownership.

Theme: Love and Equality

Brontë presents love as requiring equality. Jane’s equality speech (“it is my spirit that addresses your spirit”) demands recognition at the level of the soul. The novel rejects three false models of love: Rochester’s first proposal (love without honesty), St John’s proposal (marriage without love), and Blanche Ingram’s pursuit (marriage for money). Only when Jane and Rochester meet as equals — financially, emotionally, and morally — can their love be fulfilled.

Jane occupies the painful middle ground of the governess class: educated but dependent, refined but powerless. She challenges class assumptions throughout: “Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and little, I am soulless and heartless?” Brontë argues that moral worth transcends social rank. The Gardiners in Pride and Prejudice make the same argument through quiet respectability; Jane makes it through passionate confrontation.

The inheritance resolves the class barrier, but Brontë ensures that Jane’s moral claim to equality is established before she gets money. Her worth is proven by character, not by fortune. The money simply removes the practical obstacle.

Theme: Religion and Morality

Brontë presents three flawed models of religion (Brocklehurst’s hypocrisy, Helen’s passivity, St John’s cold duty) and asks: what is the right way to live? Jane’s answer is personal conscience. She follows her own moral compass rather than any institution or authority figure. When she says “I will keep the law given by God” while leaving Rochester, she means God’s law as she understands it — not as any clergyman interprets it.

Most 19th-century prose questions give you a printed extract and ask you to write about the extract and the wider novel. You will be assessed against the standard GCSE English Literature assessment objectives — AO1 (response with quotations), AO2 (language, form, structure analysis), AO3 (context), and AO4 (written accuracy). Spend a few minutes reading and annotating the extract before writing. Structure: 4–5 paragraphs. Paragraph 1–2: close analysis of the extract (language, technique, imagery). Paragraph 3–4: broaden to the wider novel, connecting the extract’s themes to other key moments. Final paragraph: conclude with a direct answer to the question. Embed context throughout — never as a standalone paragraph. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for exact mark weightings and timings.

Quotation bank for Jane Eyre: “Unjust! — unjust!” (defiance), “I am no bird” (freedom), “Women feel just as men feel” (feminism), “Do you think I am soulless?” (equality), “I care for myself” (integrity), “Reader, I married him” (agency), “I was in the middle before I knew that I had begun” (Rochester’s growth). Learn them all.

Key Fact

GCSE English Literature responses are assessed against four AOs: AO1 (response with quotations), AO2 (language, form, structure analysis), AO3 (context), and AO4 (written accuracy). Top-band responses embed all four within every paragraph and show awareness of the whole text, not just the extract.

Quotation Revision

Practise linking each quotation to multiple themes. “I am no bird; and no net ensnares me” connects to independence (Jane rejects confinement), feminism (women are not to be caged), and love (she will not be a kept creature). The best exam responses use a single quotation to discuss several ideas, showing the examiner that you understand how themes interconnect.

title: Character Analysis
content_html:
Dr Henry Jekyll

Jekyll is a wealthy, respected doctor who appears to be a model Victorian gentleman. He is “a large, well-made, smooth-faced man of fifty, with something of a slyish cast perhaps, but every mark of capacity and kindness.” The word “slyish” is crucial — even in this positive description, Stevenson hints at something hidden. Jekyll’s tragedy is not that he is evil but that he is human: he contains both good and evil and cannot accept this duality. His experiment is an attempt to be respectable and indulge his desires — to have it both ways without moral consequences.

Jekyll is ultimately a tragic figure. His flaw is not vice but the desire to escape moral accountability. He wants to sin without guilt, to be Hyde without being Hyde’s consequences. His confession reveals genuine self-knowledge (“I was in no sense a hypocrite”) but also self-deception (“I can be rid of Mr Hyde whenever I choose”). The gap between his self-knowledge and his self-deception is what destroys him.

Key Fact

Jekyll has genuine self-knowledge (“both sides of me were in dead earnest”) but also dangerous self-deception (“I can be rid of Mr Hyde whenever I choose”). He understands his duality intellectually but cannot control it practically. This makes him a tragic figure: he sees the truth but cannot act on it. His experiment is an attempt to cheat morality, and it destroys him.

Mr Edward Hyde

Hyde is described through other characters’ reactions because Stevenson never gives a detailed physical description. He is “pale and dwarfish,” gives an “impression of deformity without any nameable malformation,” and provokes instant revulsion. His violence escalates from cold indifference (trampling the child) to savage fury (the Carew murder). Hyde represents the id — the selfish, instinctive part of human nature freed from conscience.

Utterson is described as “ausere with himself” — he suppresses his own pleasures (he drinks gin to mortify his taste for wine, and has not visited a theatre for twenty years). He represents the ideal Victorian gentleman: loyal, discreet, and restrained. But his very discretion is part of the problem. He suspects something is wrong with Jekyll for months but does not ask the right questions because Victorian propriety forbids intrusion into another gentleman’s private affairs.

Utterson also functions as the reader’s proxy: we discover information as he does. His rational, legal mind makes him a reliable narrator, but his Victorian restraint means he cannot see what is right in front of him. Stevenson uses Utterson to show how respectability itself becomes an obstacle to truth.

Lanyon dismissed Jekyll’s work as “unscientific balderdash” before the events of the novella. He represents conventional Victorian science — empirical, cautious, and unwilling to explore dangerous territory. When he witnesses the transformation, the shock kills him. Lanyon is Stevenson’s comment on the limits of the conventional Victorian worldview: it can function only as long as certain truths remain hidden. Once exposed, it shatters.

Lanyon and Jekyll are foils: Jekyll pushes beyond accepted boundaries while Lanyon stays safely within them. Both are destroyed — Jekyll by his recklessness and Lanyon by the truth he refused to consider. Stevenson suggests there is no safe position: ignoring human duality is as dangerous as confronting it.

Key Fact

Each character represents a different response to duality: Jekyll (attempts to separate good and evil), Hyde (evil without conscience), Utterson (refuses to look too closely), Lanyon (destroyed by the truth he cannot accept). Together, they explore the Victorian dilemma: how do you live with the knowledge that civilised people contain primitive impulses?

title: Key Themes
content_html:
Theme 1: Racism and the Care System

The novel’s central theme is structural racism — specifically, how racist outcomes can be produced by systems that do not see themselves as racist. The care system does not explicitly state that white babies are worth more than mixed-race children. But its processes, priorities, and outcomes reveal exactly that hierarchy.

Key Fact

De Waal shows racism as structural rather than individual. No single character says anything overtly racist. Instead, racism operates through processes: who is considered ‘adoptable,’ whose needs are prioritised, whose family bonds are valued. This is more insidious — and harder to challenge — than individual prejudice.

The separation of Leon and Jake is the novel’s sharpest critique. Jake is adopted because the system has white families waiting for white babies. Leon is fostered because the system lacks equivalent demand for mixed-race older children. Neither social worker is personally racist — but the outcome is racist. De Waal forces the reader to confront how bias can be built into institutions.

Racism in the novel extends beyond the care system. Leon encounters it in school, on the streets, and in the wider community. The social hierarchies of 1981 Birmingham place Black and mixed-race people at the bottom, denied equal access to housing, employment, and justice.

The Handsworth riots represent the community’s collective refusal to accept this position any longer. De Waal connects the personal (Leon’s separation from Jake) to the political (a community rising against structural oppression) to show that individual suffering and collective injustice have the same root cause.

Theme 2: Family and Separation

De Waal interrogates what ‘family’ means through multiple models: the birth family (Carol, Leon, Jake), the foster family (Maureen), the adoptive family (Jake’s new parents), and the wider community. The novel argues that bonds are created through love and presence, not biology alone — but also that severing existing bonds causes permanent damage.

Key Fact

The novel’s most powerful argument is that sibling bonds matter. The system treats Jake’s placement as a success — he has a stable, affluent home. But it ignores the severed connection to Leon. De Waal suggests that material provision is not the same as emotional wholeness, and that the system’s definition of ‘best interests’ is dangerously narrow.

Theme 3: Identity and Belonging

Leon’s identity is fractured by the system. He is mixed-race in a society that sees race in binary terms. He belongs to a white mother and a Black community. He is neither fully one thing nor another — and the system has no category for this complexity.

Maureen provides cultural anchoring that the care system cannot. Through her, Leon gains access to Caribbean food, music, language, and community. This gives him a sense of belonging that the white institutional world has denied. De Waal suggests that identity is not innate but constructed through relationships and cultural immersion.

De Waal makes identity political. In 1981, mixed-race children in care were often placed with white families who could not help them develop a positive racial identity. The result was children who felt they belonged nowhere. Maureen’s role in the novel is partly a corrective to this — showing what culturally competent care looks like.

Leon’s name is itself significant. The title, My Name is Leon, is a statement of selfhood — a refusal to be reduced to a case number, a ‘placement,’ or a category. By insisting on his name, Leon insists on his individual humanity within a dehumanising system.

Theme 4: Childhood, Neglect and Innocence

The novel explores how neglect robs children of childhood. Leon should be playing, learning, and being carefree. Instead, he is feeding a baby, navigating social workers, and searching for his brother. De Waal shows that poverty and parental illness force children into premature adulthood — not because children are incapable, but because they should not have to be capable.

Yet Leon retains elements of childhood throughout: his love of the garden, his concrete thinking, his inability to grasp abstract concepts like ‘permanency.’ De Waal preserves his innocence even as the world strips it away. This tension between what Leon should be (a child) and what he is forced to become (a carer, a fighter, a survivor) generates the novel’s emotional power.

Theme 5: Class and Poverty

Class operates alongside race throughout the novel. Carol is working-class, unemployed, and without support networks. Jake’s adoptive family is middle-class and comfortable. The care system implicitly values material provision over emotional bonds — a middle-class home with two parents and a garden is deemed ‘better’ than a loving sibling relationship in a poorer setting.

De Waal shows how multiple forms of disadvantage intersect. Carol is disadvantaged by class (working-class), gender (single mother bearing sole responsibility), and circumstance (mental health, absent partners). Leon is disadvantaged by race (mixed-race), age (too old to be easily adopted), and family background (mother in crisis).

The novel argues that these disadvantages are not accidental but systemic. Thatcher’s Britain created conditions where working-class families were more likely to break down and Black children were more likely to be failed by the resulting care system. Individual suffering is connected to political choices.

Theme 6: The 1981 Riots — Resistance and Voice

The riots are not presented as mindless violence but as a form of political resistance. The community has been silenced, policed, and impoverished. The riot is the moment when that silence breaks. De Waal draws a direct parallel: just as Leon has been silenced by a system that does not listen to children, the Black community has been silenced by a state that does not listen to its citizens.

The novel suggests that when legitimate channels fail — when complaints are ignored, when the system does not change — eruption is inevitable. This applies to both the community (rioting) and Leon (acting out). De Waal does not condone violence, but she refuses to condemn it without acknowledging its causes.

title: Chapters 4–6: The Carew Murder and Incident at the Window
content_html:
Chapter 4: The Carew Murder Case

Nearly a year after the events of Chapter 2, Hyde commits a far more serious crime. A maid witnesses him brutally beating an elderly gentleman — Sir Danvers Carew, a respected MP — to death with a heavy walking stick. The attack is unprovoked: Carew had simply asked Hyde for directions.

The violence is extreme. The maid describes how Hyde “broke out in a great flame of anger” and “clubbed him to the earth” with “ape-like fury.” The cane snaps in half under the force of the blows. Stevenson uses this scene to show that Hyde’s evil is escalating — from trampling a child to committing murder.

Key Fact

The broken walking stick belonged to Utterson — he had given it to Jekyll as a gift years earlier. This detail physically connects Jekyll to the murder and foreshadows the eventual revelation that they are the same person.

Utterson takes the police to Hyde’s rooms in Soho. The setting is significant: Soho was one of Victorian London’s most disreputable areas, associated with poverty, crime and vice. Hyde’s rooms are furnished with luxury items but show signs of a hasty departure — ashes in the fireplace, a burnt cheque book. Hyde has vanished.

Stevenson describes Soho in fog and darkness: “a district of some city in a nightmare.” The symbolism is clear — Soho represents the hidden, immoral side of London that respectable Victorians preferred to ignore. The fog that blankets the streets mirrors the moral confusion surrounding Jekyll’s double life.

Chapter 5: The Letter

Utterson visits Jekyll, who is visibly shaken. Jekyll claims he has received a letter from Hyde promising to disappear forever. Jekyll asks Utterson to judge whether the letter should be given to the police. Utterson agrees to keep it.

Later, Utterson’s clerk Mr Guest notices that the handwriting in Hyde’s letter is remarkably similar to Jekyll’s own handwriting — just slanted differently. Utterson is horrified: “Henry Jekyll forge for a murderer!” He assumes Jekyll is covering for Hyde, not yet suspecting the truth.

Key Fact

The matching handwriting is a crucial clue that Jekyll and Hyde are the same person. Stevenson plants this evidence for the reader, but Utterson — bound by Victorian propriety — refuses to follow it to its logical conclusion.

Chapter 6: Remarkable Incident of Dr Lanyon

Time passes. Hyde has disappeared, and Jekyll seems renewed — sociable, charitable and “at peace.” For two months, he appears to have conquered his demons. But then Jekyll suddenly withdraws from society, refusing all visitors.

When Utterson visits Dr Lanyon, he finds him shockingly changed — pale, thin and visibly dying. Lanyon says he has received “a shock” from which he will never recover. He refuses to discuss Jekyll, saying only: “I wish to see or hear no more of Dr Jekyll … I am quite done with that person.”

Lanyon’s transformation is one of the novella’s most powerful moments. A once-confident, robust man has been reduced to a dying shell. Stevenson withholds the cause of his horror — we only learn what Lanyon witnessed in Chapter 9. This delayed revelation builds suspense and suggests that the truth is so terrible it literally kills the man who sees it.

Lanyon dies shortly afterwards. He leaves Utterson a sealed letter, only to be opened after Jekyll’s death or disappearance. Utterson — ever the man of principle — respects Lanyon’s wishes and does not open it.

Stevenson uses sealed letters as a structural device throughout the novella. Jekyll’s will, Lanyon’s letter and Jekyll’s own “full statement” are all documents that contain the truth but are withheld from the reader. This creates a pattern of secrets and revelations that mirrors the theme of hidden identity.

title: Chapters 4-6: The Beast & the Breakdown
content_html:
Chapter 4: Painted Faces and Long Hair

Chapter 4 marks a turning point in the novel. The title itself — “Painted Faces and Long Hair” — signals the boys’ physical transformation away from civilisation. Their hair has grown wild, their clothes are ragged, and crucially, Jack discovers the power of face paint. He smears his face with coloured clay and charcoal and looks at his reflection in a pool of water. What he sees transforms him: “He looked in astonishment, no longer at himself but at an awesome stranger.”

The mask of paint is one of Golding’s most powerful symbols. It dehumanises Jack — he is no longer himself but a “stranger.” Behind the mask, he is freed from the shame and guilt that civilisation imposes. The paint allows him to act without conscience. Golding writes that the mask “compelled them,” suggesting it has its own power — once the boys adopt these new identities, they are no longer in control of their own behaviour. This reflects Golding’s belief that civilised identity is a construct that can be stripped away.

Key Fact

Jack’s face paint represents the destruction of civilised identity. Behind the mask, he becomes an “awesome stranger” — freed from shame, guilt and personal responsibility. Golding suggests that removing individual identity is the first step towards savagery.

Roger and the Stones: The Taboo of Civilisation

One of the most significant moments in Chapter 4 is easily overlooked. Roger follows a littlun called Henry to the beach and begins throwing stones at him — but deliberately misses, aiming to land them in a circle around the child rather than hitting him. Golding explains why: “Roger’s arm was conditioned by a civilisation that knew nothing of him and was in ruins.”

This is one of the novel’s most important lines. Roger wants to hurt Henry but is still held back by the invisible taboo of the old world — the memory of parents, teachers, police, punishment. That civilisation is described as knowing “nothing of him” and being “in ruins” tells us that this restraint is fading. Roger’s arc from throwing stones near Henry to rolling a boulder onto Piggy in Chapter 11 traces the complete erosion of civilised restraint. He becomes the novel’s most chilling character because his cruelty is deliberate, escalating, and ultimately unchecked.

Roger is Golding’s study of how ordinary people become capable of atrocity. In Chapter 4, he throws stones but misses deliberately. By Chapter 6, he is one of Jack’s most loyal followers. By Chapter 11, he deliberately levers a boulder onto Piggy, killing him. In Chapter 12, he “sharpened a stick at both ends” — implying he intends to put Ralph’s head on a stake like the pig’s. Each step is a further removal of civilised restraint.

Golding’s wartime experience is crucial context here. He witnessed ordinary men commit terrible acts when the structures of law and consequence were removed. Roger is not a born psychopath — he is a schoolboy whose capacity for cruelty is unleashed by the absence of adult authority. This is Golding’s most disturbing argument: that the potential for evil exists in everyone.

The Missed Rescue

The novel’s most devastating early scene comes when a ship passes the island while the signal fire has gone out. Jack and his hunters, responsible for maintaining the fire, abandoned their duty to hunt a pig. They return triumphant, chanting “Kill the pig. Cut her throat. Spill her blood” — covered in blood and intoxicated by their first kill. Ralph is furious: they have sacrificed their best chance of rescue for the thrill of hunting.

This moment crystallises the novel’s central conflict. The signal fire represents civilisation, cooperation and hope; the hunt represents savagery, dominance and immediate gratification. Jack cannot understand Ralph’s anger because his values have already shifted. The kill was more important to him than rescue. Golding structures this scene as a point of no return — after this, the hunters’ loyalty to Jack deepens, and Ralph’s authority weakens irreversibly.

Key Fact

The hunters’ chant — “Kill the pig. Cut her throat. Spill her blood” — transforms hunting from a practical activity into a savage ritual. The rhythmic, imperative verbs create an almost hypnotic quality. The chant bonds the hunters into a tribe and replaces rational thought with collective violence.

Chapter 5: Beast from Water

Ralph calls an assembly to confront the deteriorating situation. The shelters are falling apart, boys are defecating in the wrong places, and nobody maintains the fire. Ralph tries to reimpose order: “The rules are the only thing we’ve got!” But the assembly collapses when the littluns’ fear of the beast takes over the discussion. Jack dismisses Ralph’s rules — “Bollocks to the rules!” — and promises to hunt the beast down. Fear, not reason, is now driving the group.

It is during this assembly that Simon tries to express a profound truth. He suggests that “maybe there is a beast… maybe it’s only us.” The other boys laugh at him. Simon’s insight — that the beast is not an external creature but the darkness within each boy — is the novel’s central revelation. But Golding shows that truth-tellers are ridiculed and eventually destroyed. Simon’s inability to articulate his idea clearly mirrors how difficult it is to confront uncomfortable truths about human nature.

A dead parachutist lands on the mountain during the night. Sam and Eric, tending the signal fire, see the body moving in the wind and flee in terror, convinced they have seen the beast. The boys organise a search party. They explore Castle Rock — a narrow, rocky outcrop at the end of the island. Jack is immediately drawn to it: “What a place for a fort!” He sees its military potential, not as shelter but as a seat of power.

Castle Rock contrasts sharply with the open beach where Ralph holds assemblies. The beach is democratic, exposed, communal. Castle Rock is defensible, exclusive, and threatening — a place suited to a dictatorship, not a democracy. Its later significance as Jack’s headquarters is foreshadowed here. Golding is mapping geography onto political systems: open spaces foster debate; fortresses foster tyranny.

Fear as a Tool of Power

Chapters 4–6 show how fear becomes a political tool. Jack cannot defeat Ralph through argument, so he exploits the boys’ fear of the beast instead. By promising to protect them from the beast through hunting, Jack offers an emotional solution that Ralph’s rational approach cannot match. Jack declares: “The thing is — fear can’t hurt you any more than a dream.” Yet he simultaneously encourages fear to consolidate his own power. This paradox is central to Golding’s critique: authoritarian leaders need fear. They create it, sustain it, and offer themselves as the only solution.

title: Act 5: Peace & Marriage
content_html:
Henry Woos Katherine (Act 5, Scene 2)

After the military triumph at Agincourt, Shakespeare shifts to a radically different register. Act 5, Scene 2 is an extended wooing scene in which Henry attempts to win Princess Katherine of France. He presents himself as a “plain soldier” who “cannot look greenly, nor gasp out my eloquence” — but this claim of simplicity is itself a rhetorical strategy. The audience has watched Henry deliver some of the most eloquent speeches in English literature; his pretence of plain-speaking is a deliberate performance designed to seem sincere.

The scene mixes English and French, creating comic confusion as Henry and Katherine struggle to communicate. Shakespeare uses the language barrier to generate humour, but it also carries serious implications. Katherine has very little genuine choice: the marriage is a political necessity sealed by the Treaty of Troyes. Her consent is a formality. When Henry says “you and I cannot be confined within the weak list of a country’s fashion,” he is both charming and presumptuous — he assumes his will overrides both custom and Katherine’s own preferences.

Key Fact

Henry claims to be a “plain soldier” who cannot speak eloquently — but the audience knows he is the play’s supreme rhetorician. His pretence of simplicity is itself a performance. The wooing scene shows Henry code-switching once more: he uses a different register for love than for war, but both are calculated to achieve his objective.

The Treaty of Troyes

The marriage is sealed by the Treaty of Troyes, which makes Henry heir to the French throne. The French King agrees to all of Henry’s terms — not because of the wooing scene but because of the military defeat at Agincourt. Love and politics are inseparable: the marriage is both a personal union and a political dynastic alliance. Katherine is exchanged between nations in much the same way that Hero is exchanged between men in Much Ado — her consent is assumed, not genuinely sought.

Shakespeare presents the peace as fragile. The French King blesses the marriage with hopes that “English may as French, French Englishmen, / Receive each other.” But the audience already knows — from the Henry VI plays and from the Epilogue about to come — that this peace will not last. Henry’s triumph is temporary. Everything he has won will be lost by his son.

The Chorus returns for the Epilogue in sonnet form. The message is devastating: Henry V “lived but a short time” and his son, Henry VI, “lost France and made his England bleed, / Which oft our stage hath shown.” The reference to Shakespeare’s own Henry VI plays reminds the audience that they already know the ending of this story. The glory of Agincourt is framed by futility. Shakespeare refuses to let the play end on simple celebration: triumph and loss are inseparable, and the cycle of war continues.

Katherine’s Agency

Katherine is one of the play’s most debated characters. Her English lesson scene (Act 3, Scene 4) is charming and comic — she practises English words with her gentlewoman Alice, and the scene ends with double entendres that would have delighted Shakespeare’s audience. But the comedy conceals a serious point: Katherine is preparing herself for a future she cannot control. She will be given to the English king regardless of her own wishes. In the wooing scene, she speaks very little and mostly in French; Henry dominates the conversation. Her final consent — “Dat is as it shall please de roi mon père” (it is as my father the king shall please) — defers to her father’s authority, not her own desire.

Key Fact

Katherine’s consent — “as it shall please de roi mon père” — defers to her father, not her own desire. Like Hero in Much Ado, Katherine is exchanged between men as a political commodity. Shakespeare presents the marriage as both romantic and transactional, refusing to simplify the relationship between love and power.

The tonal shift from Agincourt’s carnage to the wooing scene’s comedy is deliberately jarring. Shakespeare moves from the death of the Boy and the order to kill prisoners straight into Henry’s playful courtship. This juxtaposition forces the audience to question the relationship between war and its supposed rewards: is the marriage a happy ending or a political transaction imposed on a defeated nation? The Epilogue then undercuts even this ambiguous happiness by reminding the audience of what comes next. Shakespeare structures Act 5 to deny the audience simple satisfaction.

The difficulty of communication between English and French. It generates comedy but also symbolises the gap between political reality and personal connection.
Adapting language and register to suit different audiences. Henry speaks differently to soldiers, enemies and Katherine.
The joining of two kingdoms through marriage. Henry’s marriage to Katherine unites England and France.
A fourteen-line poem. Shakespeare uses the sonnet form for the Epilogue, giving the play a formal, contained ending.
